questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero
questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-2}^{2}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-3}^{6}5{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-9}^{9}2{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=3{x}^{2}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =3(-x)^{2} \\  & =3{x}^{2} \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)=5{x}^{3}$ is an odd function, but integral II is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}g(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

- The function $h(x)=2{x}^{5}$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =2(-x)^{5} \\  & =-2{x}^{5} \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-9}^{9}2{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero
questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-2}^{2}x({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(-x)) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-4x) \\  & ={x}^{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)) \\  & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $g(x)=x({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)({e}^{(-x)}+{e}^{-(-x)}) \\  & =-x({e}^{-x}+{e}^{x}) \\  & =-x({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}) \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}x({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $h(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(-x)) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2x) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) \\  & \ne -h(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=x{e}^{{x}^{4}}$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x){e}^{(-x)^{4}} \\  & =-x{e}^{{x}^{4}} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=x{e}^{{x}^{4}}$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}x{e}^{{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

$$
